name: Pedro Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for sitting down with me. I'm a senior field researcher at the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy screws, bolts, hinges and fixings for Hartley Fixings, a distributor with about sixty staff and a warehouse on Canal Road. I lead a team of three junior buyers, so my morning is supplier calls, checking last week's stock gaps and haggling over a price per thousand. After lunch it's quotes for builders' merchants and a lot of emails I'd rather not answer.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the haggling, honestly. A good supplier and I have been trading favours for years, and I know which factory will slip a delivery before they do. What wears me out is the new purchasing software the managing director, Stuart, keeps pushing, because it adds screens and takes away judgement. My partner Rita is a nurse on shifts, so we also live on a tight rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AI Plateau". Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say, told you so, it's mostly a fancy spreadsheet. The union meeting would have a good laugh. Online I'd probably keep quiet, because I don't want to be the guy who gloats.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my job stays mine for now, which is a relief. But I still don't trust Stuart, because he'll use the hype as a reason to hold down pay. Our rent went up last spring, so a quiet year isn't the same as a safe one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do. I'd push for the pay rise I've been promised since March and keep topping up the savings, about two hundred a month. I'd also keep going to the union branch on Thursdays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly steady, if I'm honest. A bit bored, a bit annoyed that the company wastes money on software that does little. There's a small knot about rent, but that's not about AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't use AI tools at all. Is that a rule or just habit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's habit with a bit of principle. I don't like handing my supplier notes to a company I can't see. And when I tried a chatbot once for a quote email, it invented a price, which proved my point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the plateau do to the three juniors on your team?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd be fine. They'd still learn the phones and the supplier names, and I'd keep teaching them how to read a quote. I'd worry more about Stuart cutting the junior hiring to pay for the software.

say: I'd tell colleagues it's **mostly hype**, a fancy spreadsheet, and I'd say it loudly at the union meeting.
Online I'd keep quiet and **not gloat**, since the software could still land on my desk.
think: My job stays mine for now, but I don't trust **Stuart** not to use the hype to hold pay down.
Rent rose last spring, so even a **quiet year** is still a squeeze.
do: Push for the **overdue pay rise** promised since March and keep up the union Thursdays.
Save about **200 a month** towards a bigger cushion for the flat.
feel: Steady but irritated, with a small knot about **rent** that has nothing to do with AI.
S0.quote: Our rent went up last spring, so a quiet year isn't the same as a safe one.
fieldNote: Pedro is blunt and wary; his unease comes from **rent** and a boss he doesn't trust, not from AI itself.
He refuses AI tools on **principle** and a bad experience with an invented price backs it up.

steps.text: Ask Stuart for the overdue pay rise before the spring review
Put 200 a month into the savings account for the flat
Attend the Thursday union branch meetings and raise the pay talks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "Steady Disruption". Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the owners' choice, not the machine's. Software doesn't decide to skip hiring juniors, Stuart does. At the union I'd call for a written agreement that nobody loses their job because of a purchasing tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's about me. Reordering the standard lines, chasing delivery dates, comparing three quotes: that's half my day and a program can do it. What it can't do yet is phone a factory manager and hear in his voice that something is wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd stop hiding from it and sit in on the demo, just to see what it gets wrong. I'd write down every error. And I'd push the union to ask for a retraining budget, paid hours, so nobody has to learn it on their own evening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit scared, and angry about being scared. I've worked hard to be among the best at this, and the thing I'm best at is the thing that gets automated first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Buying is one of the tasks on that card. What does it look like on your own desk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On my desk, the reorders go first. The juniors would watch the system place orders and I'd be the person who explains why it's wrong, which sounds important until Stuart asks why he needs four of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame if the juniors get squeezed out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The owners and the investors behind them, not the juniors and not the supplier reps. If a company saves money on thinking work, the savings should help the people doing it, with shorter weeks or a bonus, not just a higher dividend.

say: It's the **owners' choice**, not the machine's, and I'd demand a written promise that no one loses a job to a tool.
Software doesn't decide to skip hiring juniors; **Stuart** does.
think: Half my day is **reorders and quote comparisons**, and a program can do that.
My edge is the **phone call** where I hear a factory manager's voice and know something is wrong.
do: Sit in on the demo and write down **every error** the system makes.
Push the union for **paid retraining hours**, so nobody learns it on their own evening.
feel: **Scared** and angry about being scared, because my best skill is the one aimed at first.
S1.quote: I've worked hard to be among the best at this, and the thing I'm best at is the thing that gets automated first.
fieldNote: His anxiety is concrete: the **reorder work** that fills half his day is the work the card names.
He still frames it as a fight over who benefits, which is where his **union** politics show.

steps.text: Sit through the purchasing software demo and log every mistake it makes
Ask the union branch to demand paid retraining hours in writing
Back the party that wants a shorter working week when companies automate

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2028". Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need emergency rules, and I'd say it everywhere. A two-year warning is no warning, and the government hasn't even settled how to tax a robot. At work I'd be the one standing up in the canteen asking what the plan is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job goes first. A buyer is a thinking job on a screen, and I'd guess most of the team would be gone within a year of it arriving. Rita's hospital work is safer, but one nurse's pay doesn't cover our rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd empty every spare pound into savings and stop going out. I'd look for any job with my hands or with people, maybe warehouse supervision, because that has three extra years. And I'd lean on the union for a redundancy deal while it still has weight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, mostly. Not dramatic, just a heavy feeling in the stomach each Monday. I'd lie awake doing the maths on four months of savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is very short. What do you do on day one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Day one, I'd sit down with Rita and put every bill on the table. Then I'd go to Stuart and ask for a meeting with the whole team, because I'd rather hear the bad news from him than from a rumour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the three-year gap before robots matter for you at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It matters a lot. I'm a desk buyer, so I'm on the early side, but the warehouse next door has three more years. That's why supervising on the floor looks like a lifeboat to me, though lifeboats get crowded.

say: We need **emergency rules**, and I'd say so in the canteen: two years' warning is no warning at all.
Nobody has even settled how to **tax a robot**.
think: A buyer is a screen job, so I'd expect **most of us gone** within a year of it arriving.
Rita's nursing pay alone won't cover our **rent**.
do: Put every spare pound into **savings** and stop eating out.
Look at **warehouse supervision**, since hands-on work gets about three extra years.
feel: **Sick** and heavy each Monday, lying awake doing the sums on four months of savings.
S2.quote: I'd lie awake doing the maths on four months of savings.
fieldNote: Pedro expects to lose the job and says so plainly; his composure is **anger**, not calm.
The robot delay is his **lifeboat** idea, and he knows others will think of it too.

steps.text: Move every spare pound into savings and stop eating out
Cancel the gym and the streaming subscriptions this month
Apply for warehouse supervisor jobs at the depots across town
Press the union for a redundancy deal before layoffs begin

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2031". Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same thing, only calmer: we've got time, so let's use it. I'd push for a retraining fund and a national plan, and I'd tell friends to start moving now instead of waiting for the news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be mid-career when it lands, around thirty-two. That's frightening but not hopeless. Five years is enough to change direction if I start in the first one, and if I wait I'll be panicking in the last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start with an evening course in logistics management, the hands-on side, with warehouse and fleet planning. I'd also save aggressively and ask the union to bargain for training days. And I'd finally look at what the purchasing software does, so I'm not ignorant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but workable. It's like knowing a storm is coming and having a few days to board up the windows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years gives a little room. What would you actually use it for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use it to build a second skill that isn't a screen. That's why logistics. And to get Rita and me out of rent into something steadier, if we can ever manage a deposit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you feel about studying again at that point?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine with it, even keen. I did a master's and liked it. My worry is that I'd be a thirty-year-old student next to twenty-year-olds, but I've got over that sort of pride.

say: We have time, so let's **use it**: I'd call for a national retraining fund and tell friends to start now.
Waiting for the news is the **wrong plan**.
think: I'd be about thirty-two when it lands, which is frightening but **not hopeless**.
Five years only works if I **start straight away**.
do: Enrol in an evening course in **logistics management**, the hands-on warehouse and fleet side.
Ask the union to bargain for **paid training days** and save harder.
feel: **Uneasy** but workable, like having a few days to board up the windows before a storm.
S3.quote: Five years is enough to change direction if I start in the first one, and if I wait I'll be panicking in the last.
fieldNote: Pedro treats the time as a **deadline**, not a comfort, and his plan is already specific.
Studying again doesn't bother him; he has dropped the **pride** that might hold others back.

steps.text: Enrol in an evening logistics management course starting in January
Raise the savings pot from four months to eight months of rent
Ask the union to bargain for paid training days

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2036". Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift and we should treat it like one. Companies like Hartley should be made to put money aside now, because later they'll cry poverty. At the union I'd want it written into the next three agreements.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd relax a lot. I'd be thirty-seven, and I could plan a life around it: kids maybe, a flat of our own. The hard part is that I'd know it's coming and still have to sit in a job I can't fully trust to last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job and my union role, and I'd learn the software properly, no sulking. I'd save for a deposit and have a second qualification by thirty. If Rita and I decide on a child, I'd do it knowing we've got a plan, not a panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer than the others. There's still a worry, but it's the ordinary kind, the kind you can live next to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, does the pressure ease or just move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It eases the fear and moves it to fairness. Ten years of planning is only a gift if employers and the state actually pay for it. If they don't, the people with savings will be fine and the rest won't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think should pay for people to change careers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Employers first, since they're the ones saving the money, and the state with a tax on that saving. Not individual workers out of their own pocket, because that's how a hard change turns into a class divide.

say: Ten years is a **gift**, and Hartley should set money aside now before it cries poverty later.
I'd want retraining written into the next **three union agreements**.
think: I could plan a life around it, maybe **children and a flat**, though the job still feels borrowed.
Whether the gift is real depends on **who pays** for the change.
do: Learn the purchasing software **properly**, without sulking, and keep the union role.
Save for a **deposit** and finish a second qualification by thirty.
feel: **Calmer** than in the other pictures, with the ordinary kind of worry you can live beside.
S4.quote: Ten years of planning is only a gift if employers and the state actually pay for it.
fieldNote: Time lowers Pedro's fear but raises his sense of **fairness**: who pays becomes the real question.
He links decade-long planning to **family plans**, which none of the shorter scenarios allowed.

steps.text: Learn the purchasing software properly and test it on real reorders
Save for a flat deposit over the next four years
Finish a part-time supply-chain qualification by age thirty
Plan a first child once the deposit is in place

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, AGI by 2028. I'd have two years, four months of savings and a partner whose pay can't carry us. What would help is a real redundancy deal agreed in advance, with retraining paid for by the companies that automate.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people like me aren't against technology. I'm against being told my skill is worthless by the people who profit from it. Ask the owners the hard questions too.

headlineQuote: I'm against being told my skill is worthless by the people who profit from it.
portrait: Pedro is a **27-year-old senior buyer** and union rep at a fixings distributor, living with his nurse partner Rita.
He never uses AI and distrusts it, partly on **principle** and partly after a chatbot invented a price.
He blames **owners and investors**, not machines, and wants any savings shared with the people doing the work.
His mood climbs with speed: **uneasy** in the slow worlds, **alarmed** when AGI arrives in two years.
He copes by saving, thinking about **hands-on logistics work**, and leaning on the union.
biggestWorry: The **2028 picture**, with two years' notice, four months of savings and a partner whose pay can't carry the rent.
whatWouldHelp: A **redundancy and retraining deal** agreed in advance, paid for by the companies that automate.
